rationale: The book’s identification unifies the lamp-oil texts more tightly than the dominant alternative: pure beaten olive oil for perpetual light (Ex 27:20) is kept distinct from compounded anointing oil (Ex 25:6; 30:22–33); Proverbs already pairs “oil in the dwelling of the wise” with the fool who spends it (Prov 21:20) and equates the commandment with lamp, the lived law with light, and reproofs of instruction with the way of life (Prov 6:23), while the Psalm supplies the oil-word for that very reproof (Ps 141:5). The ten-virgin mechanics—oil stored beforehand in one’s own vessel, finite, non-transferable, and to be “bought”—then fit the inward reception and tested obedience of truth/correction (Prov 7:1–3; 23:23; Ps 119:11; Jer 31:33; 1 Jn 2:4) far better than a gift that is freely given, not purchased, and not zero-sum. The Spirit remains the efficient cause (Ezek 36:27; Zech 4:6) that produces the fruit stored as oil, not the oil itself; light is simply that obedience made visible (Matt 5:16). No counter-reading accounts for the same inventory of distinctions, proverbial pairings, and narrative constraints with fewer unsupported steps.
strongest_counter_interpretation: Lamp oil symbolizes the Holy Spirit’s indwelling, anointing, or sustaining presence that keeps the believer’s lamp burning (especially in Matt 25), drawing on the oil–Spirit link in anointing texts, the oil-fed lampstand of Zech 4 interpreted by ‘not by might … but by my Spirit,’ and the perpetual sanctuary lamps of Ex 27 / Lev 24.
counter_case: Oil is repeatedly joined to the Spirit’s coming or empowerment in royal and messianic anointing (1 Sam 16:13; Isa 61:1; Acts 10:38; 2 Cor 1:21–22).
Zechariah’s lampstand is supplied by golden oil and immediately interpreted by the Spirit oracle of 4:6, inviting the equation oil = Spirit.
Popular and much evangelical preaching on the ten virgins treats the wise virgins’ reserve oil as possession of the Spirit that cannot be borrowed, matching the non-transferable detail.
Sanctuary lamps that must burn continually (Ex 27:20) are readily read typologically as the Spirit’s unfailing presence.
book_explanatory_advantages: Preserves the explicit biblical distinction between pure lamp oil and compounded anointing oil (Ex 25:6; 30), so Spirit-anointing texts do not automatically define lamp oil.
Supplies a single OT chain (Prov 6:23 + Ps 141:5 + Prov 21:20 + Prov 23:23) that already places oil, lamp, light, wise/fool, and ‘buy the truth’ in the exact configuration later used by Matthew 25.

Explains the parable’s commercial and finite language (buy, not enough for us and you, go to the sellers) without forcing the free gift of the Spirit into a zero-sum commodity that can be purchased too late.

Keeps the Spirit as cause (Ezek 36:27) while identifying the stored oil as the tested fruit of that cause—obedience formed inwardly—so light can be the visible good works of Matt 5:16 without collapsing categories.
Accounts for the fool/wise polarity already defined in the same chapter as hearers who do not versus hearers who do (Matt 7:24–27; Ps 111:10).
counter_explanatory_advantages: Offers a single, familiar referent that covers both anointing and lamp imagery for many readers.
Leans on the strong Spirit–oil association already present in several high-profile passages.
Requires fewer intermediate steps for those who treat Zech 4:6 as an immediate definition of the oil.
decisive_sources: Proverbs 21:20 (oil stored by the wise, spent by the fool)
Ezekiel 36:27 and Zechariah 4:6–14 (Spirit as power that produces walk/work, not itself called the oil)
1 John 2:4 and Proverbs 7:1–3 (truth/commandment either in or not in the man)
unresolved_objections: Some will continue to collapse lamp oil into anointing oil because both begin as olive products and both appear near Spirit language.

The full definition ‘tested, pressed fruit of the Spirit stored as proven obedience’ is a synthesis rather than a single verse’s explicit gloss, leaving room for preference for simpler labels such as ‘readiness’ or ‘grace.’
